8	We address these gaps with a multi-benchmark G-theory study \citep{shavelson1991generalizability, brennan2001generalizability} that crosses seven facets (item, model, numerical precision, prompt template, random seed, sampling temperature, and answer ordering) across eight models and five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, and MATH), totaling 2.3 million records. The central finding is that variance structure is format-conditional. All three multiple-choice benchmarks share an item-dominated structure: item selection accounts for 34--38\% of total variance, with model$\times$item interaction as the second-largest source. Free-form benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH) exhibit a different profile: model, prompt template, and item each contribute 12--24\%, with no single dominant source. The gap between MC item dominance (34--38\%) and free-form item shares (17--24\%) reflects a systematic format-dependent pattern in what drives evaluation variance. In multiple-choice settings, the item pool determines measurement reliability; in free-form settings, prompt design and model selection matter as much as item selection. A second finding is that model$\times$item interaction (up to 33\% in cross-model MMLU analysis) is the hidden second-largest variance source, larger than all methodology main effects combined. Models differ not in overall ability but in which specific items they find difficult. D-study projections translate these findings into practical design guidance: the format-conditional structure implies that reliability optimization strategies must differ between MC and free-form benchmarks. Figure~\ref{fig:cross_benchmark} visualizes the contrast across all four benchmarks.

lines: Existing studies have examined individual variance sources in isolation, each implicitly assuming separability. \citet{sclar2024formatting} documented up to 76\% accuracy swings from prompt formatting perturbations but held hardware and item selection fixed. BrittleBench \citep{brittlebench2026} found 50\% variance from prompt perturbation under the same constraint. \citet{yuan2025layercast} showed that numerical precision and GPU type cause up to 9\% accuracy variation but provided no factorial attribution to specific sources or their interactions. \citet{mesting2026hidden} applied Generalizability theory (G-theory) to LLM evaluation and decomposed variance across five methodology facets on a single benchmark; judge identity dominated at 43.8\%, but the study included no cross-benchmark comparison and excluded infrastructure facets such as numerical precision. Studies of answer ordering \citep{pezeshkpour2024ordering} and hyperparameter sensitivity \citep{dodge2020finetuning, henderson2018deep} have documented additional sources of variation, again in isolation from the factors above. Item Response Theory (IRT) approaches \citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks, lalor2019irt} model item difficulty parameters to construct efficient benchmarks but do not account for prompt, seed, or ordering facets. \citet{bouthillier2021accounting} established ANOVA-based variance decomposition as a principled template for ML reproducibility, but this work predates the LLM evaluation context where benchmark format introduces an additional structural variable. Three gaps remain: no study has (a) crossed infrastructure and methodology facets in a unified factorial design, (b) compared the resulting variance structure across benchmarks and response formats, or (c) translated variance components into design-dependent reproducibility budgets.

\section{Experiments}

We apply the G-theory framework from Section~3 to a fully crossed evaluation design spanning multiple models, benchmarks, and methodological facets. All experiments use open-weight 7--9B parameter models evaluated with vLLM~0.9.2 on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs (96GB). Binary correctness (1/0) serves as the primary outcome measure throughout; generation-based scoring avoids the log-likelihood artifacts identified by \citet{hua2025flaw}.

\subsection{Single-Model Baseline}

We first establish the variance structure within a single model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on MMLU to isolate methodological facet contributions before introducing cross-model variation.

\paragraph{Design.} The G-study crosses six facets: 200 items $\times$ 3 numerical precisions (BF16, FP16, FP32) $\times$ 6 prompt templates $\times$ 6 random seeds $\times$ 3 temperature levels (0.0, 0.3, 0.7) $\times$ 4 answer orderings, yielding 259,200 binary observations. Variance components are estimated via Henderson Method~I with bootstrap confidence intervals (1,000 resamples).

\paragraph{Results.} Under binary scoring, item difficulty (\texttt{item\_id}) accounts for 58.4\% of total variance, with the residual term contributing 23.1\%. All main facet effects are negligible ($<$1\% each): precision 0.9\%, prompt template, temperature, seed, and ordering each $<$0.5\%. The interesting structure appears in item-conditional interactions: prompt$\times$item is the largest at 5.5\%, followed by seed$\times$item (4.7\%), precision$\times$item (3.3\%), temperature$\times$item (2.9\%), and ordering$\times$item (0.8\%). This pattern indicates that methodological choices do not shift performance uniformly across items; instead, specific items are differentially sensitive to specific facets---prompt template variation produces the largest item-conditional effect.

The resulting generalizability coefficient is $G_\text{item} = 0.936$, indicating that 200 items under multi-facet conditions produce highly reliable rankings. A D-study projection shows $G \geq 0.80$ is achievable with as few as 55 items in this multi-facet design.

For text-exact-match scoring (requiring verbatim string matches), the variance structure shifts dramatically: temperature dominates at 79.7\% of variance, and $G_\text{item}$ collapses to 0.007. This metric-conditional divergence motivates our exclusive use of binary correctness for the remaining analyses.

\subsection{Cross-Model Variance}

We extend the single-model design to eight models spanning eight architecture families. A balanced BF16 subset (460,800 records) serves as the primary analysis sample, chosen because BF16 is the standard inference precision for these architectures. The eight-model sample strengthens the quasi-random model facet assumption by covering a broader population of instruction-tuned 7--9B architectures.

\paragraph{Results.} Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} presents the variance decomposition. Introducing model as a facet reshapes the structure: item difficulty drops from 58.4\% to 37.9\%, while model$\times$item interaction emerges as the second-largest component at up to 36\%. The model main effect accounts for 3--5\% on MC benchmarks and 9--11\% on free-form benchmarks, confirming that models differ primarily in \emph{which items} they find difficult rather than in overall ability level.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Variance decomposition for the cross-model MMLU design (8 models, BF16, 460,800 records). Components estimated via Henderson Method~I with 1,000-resample bootstrap CIs. $G_\text{item} = 0.896$.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrl}
\toprule
Component & Var.\% & 95\% CI \\
\midrule
\textbf{item\_id} & \textbf{37.9} & \\
\underline{model$\times$item} & \underline{30.2} & \\
residual & 25.0 & \\
model & 2.8 & \\
prompt$\times$item & 2.5 & \\
model$\times$prompt & 1.6 & \\
all others & $<$1.0 & \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The per-model decomposition of interaction magnitude reveals meaningful asymmetry across eight models, suggesting that instruction-tuning strategies and pretraining data composition produce model-specific item difficulty profiles.

\paragraph{D-study validation.} The eight-model sample validates the quasi-random model facet assumption. D-study projections from four-model subsets predicted $G = 0.893$ at eight models; the observed $G = 0.896$ confirms the projection ($\Delta = 0.003$).

\subsection{Format-Conditional Variance Structure}
\label{sec:format_conditional}

The preceding analyses use only MMLU, a multiple-choice benchmark. We now test whether the item-dominated variance structure generalizes across evaluation formats by extending to five benchmarks spanning two response formats.

HellaSwag reverses this ordering: model$\times$item (36.0\%) exceeds item difficulty (34.3\%), indicating maximal model disagreement at the item level.

-Free-form benchmarks exhibit a different variance profile. On GSM8K, variance distributes across item (16.9\%), model$\times$item (14.6\%), model$\times$prompt (12.9\%), and model (10.7\%), with no single dominant source; prompt main effect is only 5.0\%. MATH shows an intermediate pattern: item difficulty leads at 24.0\%, followed by model$\times$item (17.3\%) and model (8.5\%), closer to the MC structure but with a substantially larger residual (43.9\%).

+Free-form benchmarks differ markedly. On GSM8K, variance distributes across item (16.9\%), model$\times$item (14.6\%), model$\times$prompt (12.9\%), and model (10.7\%); prompt main effect is only 5.0\%. MATH shows an intermediate pattern: item leads at 24.0\% with model$\times$item at 17.3\%, but residual variance is substantially larger (43.9\%).
